This evening and tonight: Weather will be relatively quiet for 
one a little longer, as high pressure begins to yield to a 
strong system approaching from the west. Sunshine has been 
filtered through high clouds today. Those clouds will begin to 
thicken from the west, especially over the Cascades and northern
mountains, later tonight into early Friday. The first shower 
chances begin to touch the Cascade crest overnight, but it will 
remain dry. Lows tonight will be mostly in the 40s, with lower 
50s near the Wenatchee Area and L-C Valley.

Friday to Sunday: A strong mostly dry cold front pushes across 
the region Friday, while an upper trough dives in behind it 
Friday night into Saturday, before it gradually moves out 
Sunday. The front Friday will bring rain to the Cascades in the 
morning, especially near the crest. By late morning to afternoon
chances expand toward the eastern third of WA and ID, while the
PoPs in the Cascades start to decrease. By Friday evening the 
precipitation chances continue over the ID Panhandle and near 
the Cascade crest, but will be waning over the eastern third of 
WA so that by overnight the main risk is at the Cascade crest 
and near the Canadian border and near the Camas Prairie and
Clearwaters. Then as the trough axis start to migrate across the
region from northwest to southeast the precipitation chances 
redevelop over the near the Cascades through northeast WA and 
north ID Saturday afternoon and into central WA and the central 
ID Panhandle in the evening, before chances start peter out 
overnight into Sunday. Overall precipitation amounts are most 
centered around the mountains and very light outside of the 
mountains, so the majority of the CWA the front will pass with 
mostly dry. We will watch for some fog Saturday morning, after 
precipitation and when winds decline. The best potential is over
the sheltered valleys of northeast WA and north ID.

Snow levels start near 7-9kft Friday morning, then drop to 
5-8kft by evening with strong CAA with the cold front, then 
between 4-5.5kft by Saturday morning then moderate slightly in 
the afternoon and evening, lowest near the Cascades. This is the
main period where precipitation will fall, so snow is found in 
some of the mountain areas in between late Friday night into 
Saturday. The best chance for accumulating snow is around the 
Cascades crest, but other snow could also be found near places 
like Sherman Pass and Lookout pass. Accumulations look rather 
light in most areas. The main areas that could see a bit more is
the higher back-country mountain near the Cascades, so those 
hiking or camping there will see to monitor things and take 
precautions for snow and colder weather.

Winds will be the more widespread impact between Friday to 
Sunday. Winds start to increase Friday morning, then peak in the
afternoon to early evening. Winds will be out of the southwest,
turning west in the afternoon, at 15-25 mph with gusts of 30-40
mph possible over the Columbia Basin eastward. Localized gusts 
of 50 mph are possible, but confidence is low with probabilities
only near 10-15% per the NBM. I did increase winds above the 
NBM for the winds over the Palouse, which seems to under-do 
things. Winds start to wane Friday night, but starts to turn 
northerly over the Okanogan Valley from late evening to 
overnight into Saturday and increase to 10-20 mph with gusts to 
30 mph. By late Saturday afternoon winds throughout the 
remainder of the CWA sees winds turning north to northeast and 
increase in late evening to overnight. Winds remain strong 
through Sunday out of the northeast. Winds Sunday are forecast 
to be similar to the strength as Friday, but out of the 
northeast; but it will come with the addition of the ID in that 
stronger wind potential.

Blowing dust is in the forecast Friday and again Sunday. Friday
has the broadest blowing dust potential with winds out of the 
southwest to west. Most areas from the Waterville Plateau to 
WA/ID border have the potential, but strongest winds are 
Waterville Plateau to Upper Columbia Basin. Blowing dust 
advisories are in place from noon to 7 PM Friday for the 
potential for visibilities down to 1 mile or less. Not a lot of 
rain has fallen and not a lot is expected; last week there was 
some blowing dust that caused of impacts over the Upper Columbia
basin and not much has changed. Blowing dust is also possible 
again Sunday. So we will monitor potential impacts then too.

Temperatures will be trending down over next several days. 
Highs Friday will be in the 60s to mid-70s, then 50s to low 60s 
this weekend and some upper 30s and 40s in the mountains. Lows 
will in the 30s and 40s, with some 20s Saturday and Sunday night
(into Monday morning). Many areas could see freezing 
temperatures this weekend, especially Sunday night/Monday AM.
